01.note: In a time when the fields around Jerusalem had been ruined, the court did not know where to find wheat for the two loaves offered on Shavuot, and made a public proclamation. A deaf-mute man came forward and put one hand on his eye and the other on a door latch. Mordekhai asked the Sages whether there was a place called Ein Sokher ('eye' and 'latch') or Sokher Ayin. They checked, found such a place, and brought the wheat from its fields.
01.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that during the civil war that ruined the land, the omer barley came from Gaggot Tzerifin and the two loaves from Ein Sokher. This story, paired with the one about the omer before it, tells how the second place was found.

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: A Sage who works out the meaning of the deaf-mute's gestures.

terms.meaning: A Temple offering of two loaves of bread made from the new wheat crop, brought on the festival of Shavuot.
A person who can neither hear nor speak; here he communicates only by pointing.

02.note: Three women brought pairs of birds as offerings. One said hers was 'for my ziva', one 'for my yamma', and one 'for my ona'. The Sages took all three to be women ending a period of irregular bleeding, each owing a sin offering and a burnt offering. Mordekhai suggested instead that each had been in danger, from a flow, at sea, and through her eye, and was bringing burnt offerings; they checked and found he was right. The Gemara then says this Mordekhai is Petaḥya, the mishna's official in charge of the bird offerings, named for opening up difficult matters, and that unlike other Sanhedrin members who knew seventy languages, he could combine languages and interpret them.
02.why: The Gemara is telling stories of Mordekhai's wisdom after showing how he decoded a deaf-mute's gestures. This one, about reading ambiguous words, leads into the mishna that names him as the Temple's overseer of bird offerings.

people.name: Mordekhai
people.about: A Sage who reinterprets the women's words; the Gemara identifies him with Petaḥya, the official over the bird offerings.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Quoted on the qualifications required of members of the Sanhedrin.

terms.meaning: Pairs of doves or pigeons brought together as an offering.
A woman who has had a flow of uterine blood outside her expected period; after it ends she brings a sin offering and a burnt offering.
An offering burned entirely on the altar. Unlike a sin offering, which atones for a specific obligation, it can be brought voluntarily, for example in thanks.
The great court of the Sages. Rabbi Yoḥanan says its members had to know seventy languages so they would never hear testimony through a translator.

03.note: When the Boethusians claimed that Shavuot must always fall on a Sunday, Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai joined the debate: 'Fools! From where do you get this?' No one answered except one old man, who prattled that Moses loved Israel and, knowing Shavuot is only one day, set it after Shabbat so the people could enjoy two days in a row. Rabban Yoḥanan quoted the verse that the journey from Horeb takes eleven days, and asked why, if Moses loved Israel, he kept them in the wilderness forty years. The old man protested, 'My teacher, you dismiss me with this?' Rabban Yoḥanan replied: 'Fool! Will our perfect Torah not be as worthy as your idle talk?'
03.why: The Gemara is explaining a list of dates on which eulogies were forbidden; the days from the eighth of Nisan to the end of Passover mark when the correct date of Shavuot was restored against the Boethusians. After this exchange Rabban Yoḥanan gives a real proof from the verses.

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who challenges the Boethusians.

people.name: the elderly man
people.about: The only one of the Boethusians who answers him.

people.name: Moses
people.about: The old man claims Moses set Shavuot after Shabbat out of love for the people.

terms.meaning: A group that rejected the Sages' tradition and read 'the morrow after the day of rest' literally as Sunday, so that Shavuot would always fall on a Sunday.
The festival held seven weeks (fifty days) after the start of the omer count at Passover.

04.note: Rabbi Tarfon had raised a difficulty, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya answered it. Rabbi Tarfon fell silent, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya's face brightened. Rabbi Akiva said to him: 'Yehuda, your face brightened because you answered the elder? I will be astonished if you live long.' Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ilai, recalled that this happened about half a month before Passover; when he came back to the study hall for Shavuot and asked where Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya was, he was told that he had died.
04.why: The mishna rules that meal offerings from the new crop brought before the omer are unfit, but those brought after it and before the two loaves are fit. Rabbi Tarfon asked what the difference was, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya's answer set off this episode.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The elder who posed the question and fell silent at the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya
people.about: The younger scholar who answered Rabbi Tarfon and was pleased with himself.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rebukes Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya and predicts he will not live long.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ilai
people.about: Reports learning, at Shavuot, that Rabbi Yehuda ben Neḥemya had died.

terms.meaning: A pilgrimage festival seven weeks after Passover, when people came up to Jerusalem and the study hall.

05.note: Ulla reported, in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yehotzadak, an incident on the east bank of the Jordan in which wolves swallowed two children and excreted them. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the flesh was ritually pure.
05.why: The Gemara is asking whether palm leaves swallowed whole by an elephant count as digested, so that a basket woven from them is like a dung vessel that cannot become impure. This incident is offered as an answer, but the Gemara rejects it because flesh is soft and leaves are hard.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon bar Yehotzadak
people.about: The Sage in whose name Ulla reports it.

terms.meaning: Not carrying ritual impurity. Human remains normally impart impurity; the Sages ruled that flesh which had passed through the wolves no longer did.

06.note: The people of Laodicea needed oil and sent a messenger to buy a million maneh worth. Jerusalem sent him to Tyre, Tyre to Gush Ḥalav, and there he was sent to a man hoeing under his olive trees, who told him to wait until he finished. Seeing the man carry his tools and clear stones as he walked, the messenger thought the Jews were mocking him. But at home a maidservant brought hot water and a golden basin of oil, and the man dipped his hands and feet in it. After they ate, he measured out the oil, then another 180,000 maneh worth on credit, and came along to collect. The messenger hired every horse, mule, camel and donkey in the land; when his city came out to praise him, he told them to praise the man who came with him.
06.why: The Gemara has been discussing Tekoa, the main source of oil for meal offerings. It turns to a teaching that Moses' blessing of Asher, 'and dip his foot in oil', describes oil flowing like a spring in Asher's land, and this story shows it.

people.name: the messenger
people.about: Sent by the people of Laodicea to buy oil.

people.name: the olive grower
people.about: A man of Gush Ḥalav who looks like a poor laborer but supplies all the oil.

people.name: his maidservant
people.about: Brings him hot water and a golden basin of oil.

terms.meaning: A unit of money; the amounts in the story are given in maneh worth of oil.
A town the text places in the tribal portion of Asher.

07.note: Rabbi Elazar repeated Reish Lakish's teaching, that where the Torah says 'his hand' it means two hands, in the study hall without saying it in Reish Lakish's name. Reish Lakish heard and became angry. He challenged him: if 'his hand' means two, why does the Torah ever write 'his hands'? He raised twenty-four such verses against him, and Rabbi Elazar was silent. After Reish Lakish calmed down, he asked him why he had not answered that the rule was only about 'his hands' in the rite of placing hands.
07.why: The mishna requires placing both hands on an offering. Reish Lakish derived this from the Yom Kippur verse and made it a general rule; this episode tests that rule and narrows it to the rite of placing hands.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Taught Reish Lakish's rule without naming its source.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The author of the rule, angry at not being credited.

terms.meaning: A rite in which the person bringing an animal offering presses his hands on its head before it is slaughtered.
The house of study where the Sages taught and debated.

08.note: Once the light of the moon rose, and the priests imagined that the eastern sky was lit by the sunrise. They slaughtered the daily offering, and then had to take it out to the place of burning.
08.why: The Gemara quotes a mishna about Yom Kippur in which a lookout had to confirm that the whole eastern sky was lit, as far as Hebron, before the daily offering was slaughtered. This incident is the reason given for that practice.

terms.meaning: A lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon. It may not be slaughtered at night.
The place where offerings that had become unfit were taken to be burned.

09.note: Rabbi Beivai reported, in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name, that a mule of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household died and the Sages estimated its blood at a quarter-log. Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Bisna objected: Sages had testified that a carcass's blood is pure, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira told of wild donkeys killed to feed the king's lions, when pilgrims waded knee-deep in their blood and the Sages said nothing. Rabbi Beivai was silent. When Rabbi Zerika asked why, he said, 'How can I respond?', and quoted Rabbi Ḥanin's reading of the curse 'your life shall hang in doubt' as describing one who must buy grain a year ahead.
09.why: The discussion has been about the Sages' exact minimum measures. This incident has them measuring a quarter-log, the least amount of blood that imparts impurity, and so draws the objection that a carcass's blood imparts no impurity at all.

people.name: Rabbi Beivai
people.about: Reports the incident of the mule and cannot answer the objection.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is reported.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Bisna
people.about: Raises the objection that a carcass's blood is pure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira
people.about: Tells of the pilgrims wading in the donkeys' blood.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Asks Rabbi Beivai why he does not answer.

terms.meaning: A small liquid measure. The text gives it as the minimum amount of blood that imparts ritual impurity.
An animal that died without proper ritual slaughter; its flesh imparts ritual impurity.

09.flag: Stops in the middle of Rabbi Beivai's reply; his concluding line and Rav Yosef's resolution are in the following segments (story 85E28B).

10.note: Rabbi Beivai, explaining why he could not answer an objection, ends by saying that he is a man who relies on the baker for his bread, the most anxious of the three kinds of people in Rabbi Ḥanin's reading of the curse, and so in no state to answer. The Gemara asks what was concluded, and Rav Yosef says that Rabbi Yehuda was the halakhic decisor of the house of the Nasi and instructed them according to his own tradition, that the blood of a carcass is impure.
10.why: The question was why the Sages measured the blood of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's dead mule when a carcass's blood had been testified to be pure. Rav Yosef's answer resolves it, and the Gemara backs it with Rabbi Yehuda's report that Beit Hillel deem such blood impure from a quarter-log.

people.name: Rabbi Beivai
people.about: The Sage who could not answer the objection.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Gives the Gemara's resolution.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The halakhic decisor of the house of the Nasi, who ruled by his own tradition.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; 'the house of the Nasi' is his household.
The authority who gives rulings on Jewish law.

10.flag: Starts mid-exchange: the dead mule, the objection and Rabbi Beivai's silence are in the preceding segments (story 82B0AF), and segment 5 is the Gemara's resolution rather than narrative.

11.note: Shimon HaTzaddik foresaw his death: every Yom Kippur an old man in white had entered the Holy of Holies with him and come out with him, but this year he was in black and did not come out. After Sukkot he was ill seven days and died, naming his son Onias to serve in his place. Rabbi Meir tells that Onias's older brother Shimi, jealous, dressed Onias in a tunic and ribbon belt, stood him by the altar and told the priests it fulfilled a vow to his beloved; Onias fled the priests' threat to kill him and built an altar for idol worship in Alexandria. Rabbi Yehuda says Onias had yielded the post to Shimi, then grew jealous and played the trick on him; the priests turned on Onias, who fled and built an altar there for the sake of Heaven.
11.why: The mishna implies that the temple of Onias was not a place of idol worship. The Gemara cites this baraita in support, since in Rabbi Yehuda's version Onias builds his altar to serve God, against Rabbi Meir's version.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: Served in the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur; father of Onias, whom he named as his successor.

people.name: Onias
people.about: Son of Shimon HaTzaddik, who fled to Alexandria and built an altar there.

people.name: Shimi
people.about: Onias's brother, two and a half years older than him.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Gives the version in which Onias's altar was for idol worship.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Says it was not so, and gives the version in which the altar was for God.

terms.meaning: The altar and sanctuary Onias built in Alexandria, Egypt, outside the Temple in Jerusalem.
The innermost chamber of the Temple, entered only on Yom Kippur.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

12.note: Rabbi Meir sent Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to bring wine from the Samaritans' area. An old man met him and quoted a verse from Proverbs at him: 'And put a knife to your throat, if you are a man given to appetite.' Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reported this to Rabbi Meir, who issued a decree against them.
12.why: The Gemara asks why the Sages forbade eating meat slaughtered by Samaritans, and answers with this incident. It then explains that some Samaritans on Mount Gerizim worshipped an image of a dove, and Rabbi Meir took that minority into account.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sends his student for wine and then decrees against the Samaritans.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Meir to bring wine.

people.name: a certain elder
people.about: Warns Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar with a verse.

terms.meaning: A people living in the Land of Israel whose observance the Sages here judged unreliable.
A rule the Sages issue on their own authority to protect against a problem.

13.note: Rabbi Abbahu sent Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef to bring wine from the Samaritans' area. An old man met him and told him that the people there were not keepers of the Torah. Rabbi Yitzḥak told Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Abbahu told Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, and they did not leave the spot until they had declared the Samaritans full-fledged gentiles.
13.why: It parallels the earlier incident that led Rabbi Meir to decree against the Samaritans. The Gemara then asks what this later decree added, and answers that the earlier one was not accepted by the people, while this one was.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sends Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef for wine and passes on the report.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef
people.about: Sent to bring wine from the Samaritans.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: With Rabbi Asi, declares the Samaritans full-fledged gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: With Rabbi Ami, declares the Samaritans full-fledged gentiles.

terms.meaning: Treated in Jewish law as non-Jews; the Gemara goes on to apply this to the Shabbat rules for shared courtyards.
A people living in the Land of Israel whose observance the Sages doubted.

14.note: Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi stopped at the inn of Ya'ei and were served eggs shriveled in wine. Rabbi Zeira did not eat; Rav Asi did. Rabbi Zeira asked whether he was not worried that the dish contained demai wine, and Rav Asi said it had not crossed his mind. Rabbi Zeira reasoned that God does not let even the animals of the righteous cause a mishap, so surely Rav Asi would not have been led to eat forbidden food. He went out, looked into it, and found a teaching showing that no mishap had happened.
14.why: The Gemara has used the principle that God keeps the righteous from mishaps to argue that Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Asi ate Samaritan meat knowingly. It returns to that principle here, and then tests whether the Sages ever forbade mixtures containing demai.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Refuses the eggs, then reasons that Rav Asi could not have eaten forbidden food.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Eats the eggs without thinking about the wine.

terms.meaning: Produce bought from someone not trusted to have separated the required tithes, which must be tithed again in case it was not.
Portions of produce that must be set aside for priests, Levites and others before the rest may be eaten.

15.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz, son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law, testified before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that Rabbi Meir had eaten a vegetable leaf in Beit She'an without tithing it, and Rabbi permitted all the produce of Beit She'an on that basis. His brothers and his father's household united against him: would he permit what his fathers and their fathers had treated as forbidden? He answered from the verse about Hezekiah smashing the copper serpent Moses had made: could the righteous kings Asa and Jehoshaphat, who destroyed all idol worship, have left it standing? Rather, Hezekiah's ancestors had left him room to distinguish himself, and his own ancestors had left room for him too.
15.why: The Gemara is collecting cases for the principle that the righteous do not stumble into eating forbidden food, and treats Rabbi Meir's eating as deliberate. From Rabbi's reply it learns that a scholar who states a new ruling is not to be dismissed.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz
people.about: Son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law; testifies about what Rabbi Meir ate.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Ate an untithed vegetable leaf in Beit She'an.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; permits Beit She'an's produce and defends the ruling to his family.

terms.meaning: Portions of produce grown in the Land of Israel that must be given to priests and Levites; until they are separated the produce may not be eaten.
A town whose produce, according to this ruling, did not need tithing; the text explains Rabbi Meir held it was not sanctified as part of the Land of Israel.
The bronze snake Moses made in the wilderness, which the people later burned incense to, until King Hezekiah broke it.

16.note: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir was on his way to redeem captives when he reached the Ginai River and told it to part so he could cross. The river answered that both of them were doing their Maker's will, but his success was uncertain while the river's was certain. He threatened to decree that water would never flow in it again, and it parted. He then had it part for a man carrying wheat for Passover matza, who was doing a mitzva, and for an Arab traveling with them, so that he would not say this is how a companion is treated. Each time the river parted.
16.why: Rabbi Zeira argued that since God does not let even the animals of the righteous cause a mishap, the righteous themselves surely do not stumble. The Gemara asks what animals he meant, and begins this story of Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir, whose donkey is the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir
people.about: A Sage traveling to redeem captives, who commands a river to part.

people.name: the Ginai River
people.about: The river that argues with him and then parts.

people.name: a certain man
people.about: Carrying wheat for Passover matza.

people.name: a certain Arab
people.about: Traveling with them.

terms.meaning: Paying ransom to free people held captive, counted among the greatest of good deeds.
A commandment, or a good deed done in fulfillment of one.
Unleavened bread eaten on Passover.

17.note: After crossing the river, Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir stopped at an inn, and his hosts put barley before his donkey, but it would not eat. They sifted the barley, then picked it clean by hand, and still it refused. He suggested that perhaps the barley was not tithed; they tithed it, and the donkey ate. He said: 'This poor animal is going to do the will of its Maker, and you feed it untithed produce?'
17.why: This is the donkey Rabbi Zeira meant when he said God does not let the animals of the righteous cause a mishap. The Gemara then asks why the barley needed tithing, since grain bought for animals is exempt, and answers with a distinction from Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir
people.about: A Sage on a journey to redeem captives, whose donkey refuses untithed barley.

terms.meaning: Produce from which the portions owed to priests and Levites have not been set aside; it may not be eaten.

18.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi went out to meet Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir and invited him to dine; he accepted, and Rabbi's face beamed. He explained that he usually declined because some hosts want to but cannot afford it and some can but do not want to, while Rabbi both could and wanted to; but he was hurrying to a mitzva and would come back. On his return he passed a gate where white mules stood and said: 'The Angel of Death is in this man's house, and I will eat with him?' Rabbi offered to sell the mules, abandon them, cut their hooves or kill them, and each time he named a prohibition. As Rabbi kept pleading, a mountain rose between them. Rabbi wept, saying the righteous are greater after death than in life.
18.why: It continues the Gemara's account of Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir's journey, begun to explain Rabbi Zeira's saying about the animals of the righteous. The Elisha verse at its end is then debated by Rav Pappa and Abaye.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi'; invites Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir to dine.

people.name: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir
people.about: A Sage who rarely accepted invitations; he accepts, then refuses because of the mules.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina
people.about: Quoted by the Gemara: the righteous are greater after death, proved from Elisha's bones.

terms.meaning: The text treats them as deadly animals, likened to the Angel of Death.
A Torah prohibition, here applied to selling a dangerous animal to someone else.
The duty not to cause animals needless pain.
The prohibition on wasting or destroying things of value.

19.note: A certain woman kept trying to take dust from under Rabbi Ḥanina's feet to use in sorcery against him. He told her: 'Take it. It will not work for you, for it is written: There is none else beside Him.' The Gemara asks how this fits Rabbi Yoḥanan's saying that sorcery works against the heavenly entourage, and answers that Rabbi Ḥanina was different because his merit was great.
19.why: The Gemara is gathering sayings of Rabbi Ḥanina after quoting his warning about white mules. This episode illustrates his teaching that the verse 'There is none else beside Him' covers even sorcery.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage whom the woman tries to bewitch.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Quoted as saying sorcery works against the heavenly powers.

terms.meaning: Magic used to harm someone. Rabbi Yoḥanan reads its Hebrew name, keshafim, as saying it goes against the heavenly entourage.
The angels and powers on high that carry out God's will.

20.note: Ravina and Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, were sitting before Rav Ashi when a knife was brought to him to be checked. He told Rav Aḥa to check it, and Rav Aḥa examined it on the fingernail, on the flesh and on all three sides. Rav Ashi said to him, 'Well done', and added that Rav Kahana had said the same.
20.why: The Gemara has been listing ways to check a slaughtering knife, and gave conflicting reports of whether Rav Ashi required checking the three sides. Here he approves that full check; Rav Yeimar then argues the sides need no checking.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sitting before Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: Checks the knife at Rav Ashi's request.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The teacher who is brought the knife and approves the check.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Cited by Rav Ashi as teaching the same method.

terms.meaning: Checking a slaughtering knife for notches, which would tear rather than cut and make the slaughter invalid.
The cutting edge and the two flat faces of the blade.
